I run an auto shop. If I hire a newbie I am required to give him unemployment and workers comp. So here is the kicker. If I hire him and he turns out to be a bit if a loser and wrecks a car and gets hurt here is how it plays out. 1) My workers comp goes up for ALL of my employees costing me thousands more a year. My unemployment goes up unless I "fire" him and it is impossible to fire someone on workers comp so I lay him off to avoid a lawsuit by the government. 3) My liability insurance goes up by thousands because he wrecked a car and we have 12 employees so it goes up for all of us. In addition to that you lose money on an apprentice for the first year in this business and that is if the guy is good.

The solution: State run programs where the state takes the first years risk on the workers comp and unemployment and my only risk is the liability insurance. I can live with that. If the guy is good the state will have more skilled workers paying more taxes and less guys on welfare or going to college because they can get easy loans when they should be working a skilled trade.

I used to run a co-op training program for welfare through my business. Six employees from welfare who stayed on welfare, but worked for me. Welfare covered all expenses and I provided job training for 1 year. I could terminate at any time without question. I was surprised they agreed to it - but they did - and it was a smart move for them and me - the trainees all went on to become employees in the industry - I kept the good ones. It was like a regular job in all respects, except welfare covered everything while they were "trainees."

The welfare candidates liked it because they didn't have to do a job search while in the program - Welfare liked it because it got people off of the system once they learned actually working for a living wasn't so bad... and the skills were valuable.

A similar situation, the trainees lacked the necessary skills to be viable employees until I trained them. At the time, there were no schools that provided this training... so if I wanted employees, and I did, I had to train them myself.

Welfare would send candidates, but I was able to do a job interview to screen them - I rejected several candidates.

Later on I expanded the program to include high school students in their senior year when the local high school offered a co-op job training course - same arrangement as the welfare office. The high school candidates were hit and miss - those who wanted to learn did better than the welfare trainees, but others were actually worse slackers than the welfare people, and they would just go through the motions to get their credit.

All in all, using this technique I was able to create a lot more employment with the acquisition of real transferable skills, this also subsidized my business to a substantial degree with the free labor offsetting the training costs. Without this program, I would have hired very few, if any, of these people. As you say, the costs are simply too high.

Happened in Canada - but the welfare system is pretty much a carbon copy of the systems used in most states - they read from they same manuals.

I actually got the idea from Sweden's old welfare state system - it's generally referred to as active employment policy - as opposed to the passive systems used in most of North America.

The key is first of all, in North America, welfare state policy has difficulties with the idea of subsidizing a private enterprise - taxpayer dollars are paying for those "Trainees." Dollars are not specifically tasked inside the welfare system for this type of expenditure. Technically you could say the state is giving me public money. But the other side of the coin is this - once people get comfortable on the welfare system, and are not engaged in employment for an extended period of time - they have a tendency to become life long welfare cases.... so the costs associated with that, over several years - you can see the astronomical costs involved for the welfare state system. Understand they have millions of such cases in the system.

So, with my approach - at the time the six trainees received $50,000 in benefits, for the year + bus passes, medical, etc. But at the end of that year, they are no longer welfare people, and are trained, and either employed, or employable. They now have job experience, valuable skills, and a job reference - all to the good when looking for further work. At the end of year two, the state has already saved on the cost of last years trainees no longer being on the system - basically, those savings cover the investment for the following year. After two years, the state is investing $50,000 for year three, but will have saved $100,000 on years one and two no longer being in the system. Plus, those now employed people are now paying taxes.... so the money is even better from the public's point of view.

In year six, the state is investing $50,000 for 6 trainees, and not spending $300,000 on the 30 trainees who have graduated the program - and the taxes generated from the 30 employed graduates now far exceeds the annual program costs - the government is now turning a massive "profit" from their investment.

You see, it is possible to rapidly fix the welfare state - and in such a manner as to efficiently provide welfare clients the type of service they are actually in need of. Now, we are of course not talking of all clients in the system - there is a class of clients who are designated as genuinely unemployable - these people can never go to work - but then again - they are the people that welfare was originally designed to serve. Forcing this group to look for work is a waste of everybody's time.

My program is aimed at the able bodied and employable people on welfare, of which there are millions - people who should never have fallen that far through the cracks, as we say, only to be caught in the last available safety net - the net of last resort. These people are low in moral - and they need a boost to get them out of the pattern they are in. Active employment works well for this group, and over time it saves the public a vast fortune... not to mention the benefits offered to the business community - because after you work with someone for a full year, you have a pretty good idea if that person is the type of person you want to keep in your company.

As a further point - consider the number of welfare cases who also end up in prison - because crime is the method of acquiring more money that they learn - idle hands and all that - and the cost to the state of imprisoning each one of these is now $75,000 per inmate, per year. There are millions of these people as well. Many are employed inside the prisons, making license plates and some such - basically competing against third world pennies per hour labor - labor our own business community cannot compete with. Well, if we are going to pay the money anyways - is it not better to pay 1/3rd as much, catch those people in the welfare net and turn them back into taxpayers before they turn to crime? You know it is just good business sense all around... these businesses are now much more competitive, untrained people become skilled, public savings are geometric in nature, crime is reduced... the long term benefit to society as a whole is nearly impossible to measure. Children growing up in households with working parents instead of welfare parents - breaks the multi generational cycle of welfare dependence.

It's a win win for Capitalism - one we would be wise to embrace.
